steps: Step 1, List the people and places in a school. People: principal, teachers, librarian, nurse, guard, cleaner, students. Places: classrooms, library, playground, canteen, office, clinic. Each person and place has a job that helps students learn and stay safe.

Step 2, Plan a simple map. Draw the main gate at the bottom of the page. Put the office to the right of the gate, the library straight ahead, the playground at the top, and Class 2B on the left. Number the places 1 to 4.

Step 3, Add a key. Square = classroom, star = library, tree = playground, triangle = office. A key explains the symbols so anyone can read the map. Without a key, a reader cannot tell a library from a canteen.

Step 4, Give directions from the gate. 'Walk straight to the library. Turn left and go past the library to reach Class 2B.' Use words like straight, left, right, near and far. Check by tracing the path with your finger.
Step 5, Explain two rules with reasons. 'We do not run on the stairs because we could fall.' 'We keep the library quiet so others can read.' A rule plus a reason makes a full answer.
Step 6, Your turn: tell how to go from the main gate to the playground on this map. Model answer: 'From the main gate, walk straight past the library to reach the playground at the top of the page.'

Step 1, Name the six Gulf Cooperation Council states and their capitals: Bahrain (Manama), Kuwait (Kuwait City), Oman (Muscat), Qatar (Doha), Saudi Arabia (Riyadh) and the UAE (Abu Dhabi). The council was formed in 1981. Locate each on a map: five of them touch the Arabian Gulf, and Oman also has coasts on the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.

Step 2, Learn the UAE's seven emirates: Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah. Fujairah lies mainly on the Gulf of Oman coast, while most of the others face the Arabian Gulf. The federation was formed on 2 December 1971.

Step 3, Explain resources. Oil and natural gas are the main exports of Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Before oil, pearls, fish and dates were key. Saudi Arabia is the largest state in area, about 2.15 million square kilometres.

Step 4, Trace the old trade with India. Monsoon winds carried dhows from the Gulf to India's west coast in summer and back again in winter. Gulf traders carried dates and pearls; Indian ports sent timber, spices, rice and cloth. This shows a long link.

Step 5, Write a model answer: 'Ports like Dubai and Doha grew because they are on a sheltered coast between Asia, Africa and Europe. Ships can load oil, gas and goods, so trade brings jobs to people from many countries.'
Step 6, Your turn: name two resources of the Gulf and one old trade good. Model answer: 'Oil and natural gas are two resources, and pearls were an old trade good sold to India and beyond by dhow.'

Step 1, Start with speech. Early people shared knowledge by talking, songs and stories, which was fast but could be forgotten. Then people painted on cave walls and carved symbols. Writing arrived about 3200 BCE in Mesopotamia, with wedge marks pressed into clay tablets.

Step 2, Move to paper and print. Paper was developed in China, traditionally credited to about 105 CE. Woodblock printing produced a printed book, the Diamond Sutra, in 868 CE. Around 1450 movable metal type, used by Gutenberg in Germany, allowed many copies cheaply.

Step 3, Compare speed. Before the telegraph, a letter from one city to another could take days by horse. In 1844 the first long-distance telegraph message was sent from Washington to Baltimore in moments. From printing in 1450 to the telegraph in 1844 is 394 years.

Step 4, Build a timeline for modern tools: telephone 1876, radio from about 1900 to 1920, television in the 1920s, first computer network link 1969, and the World Wide Web in 1989 to 1991. Each tool let more people receive news faster.

Step 5, Write a model answer: 'The printing press mattered because books became cheaper, so more people learned to read. The internet goes further, because knowledge can be shared instantly across countries, though we must check what is true.'

Step 6, Your turn: say how a message travelled before and after the telephone. Model answer: 'Before, a letter went by horse or ship and took days. After 1876, people could speak at once from far away.'

Step 1, Classify with questions. By origin: biotic (forests, fish) or abiotic (minerals, water). By renewal: renewable (solar, wind) or non-renewable (coal, oil). By development: actual (in use) or potential (not yet used). Human skills and knowledge are human resources.

Step 2, Apply to examples. Crude oil: abiotic, non-renewable, actual. Wind: abiotic, renewable. Desert sunlight: renewable, and actual where solar panels already work, potential where none are built yet. Fish: biotic and renewable if not overfished.

Step 3, Calculate depletion. If a mine holds 1,000 million tonnes of coal and the country uses 50 million tonnes a year, it lasts 1,000 / 50 = 20 years. If demand rises to 100 million tonnes, it lasts only 10 years.

Step 4, List conservation measures. Reduce waste, recycle, use public transport, harvest rainwater, plant trees and shift to solar and wind. The UAE uses desalination for much of its drinking water, so saving water also saves energy.

Step 5, Write a model answer: 'Sustainable development means using resources for today's needs without harming future generations. For instance, planting a tree for each one cut keeps the forest resource renewable.'
Step 6, Your turn: classify natural gas, and say how to use less. Model answer: 'It is abiotic and non-renewable. We can use less by insulating homes and choosing solar energy.'

Step 1, Read land use data. A state has 20 million hectares in all, with a net sown area of 12 million. Net sown share = 12 / 20 x 100 = 60 percent. If forest is 3 million hectares, it is 15 percent, so the rest, 25 percent, is other uses.

Step 2, Match soil to crop. Alluvial soil of the Ganga plain suits wheat and rice. Black soil of the Deccan holds moisture and suits cotton. Red soil needs fertiliser for millets. Tea grows on well-drained hill slopes in Assam and the Nilgiris.

Step 3, Locate minerals. Iron ore is mined in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Karnataka. Coal is found mainly in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh. Bauxite, used for aluminium, is found in Odisha. These resources are unevenly spread, so transport matters.

Step 4, Explain industry location. Jamshedpur grew as an iron and steel centre because iron ore, coal and water lie close by. Suppose a plant needs about 1.5 tonnes of iron ore and 0.8 tonne of coal for 1 tonne of steel (a rough figure that varies by plant); it will locate near the heavy raw materials to cut transport cost.

Step 5, Write a model answer: 'Cotton textile mills grew in Mumbai because cotton from black soil lay nearby, a port allowed exports and the damp climate helped spinning. Industry can harm air and water, so rules for waste treatment are needed.'

Step 6, Your turn: explain why steel plants are placed near coal and iron ore. Model answer: 'These raw materials are heavy and lose weight in processing, so placing the plant near them cuts transport costs.'
